meta.dataset: AidRoute seed corridor intel — GB → France → Poland → Ukraine
meta.provenance: Operator claims derived from one anonymised validation interview with a volunteer convoy organiser (14 Aug 2026). Participant reviewed the anonymised summary and consented to its use. Transcript was rough; quotes lightly cleaned for readability, meaning preserved.
meta.anonymisation_rules: No names, organisation names, or destination cities in any UI surface. Attribution string: 'a volunteer convoy organiser'.
meta.opsec: Procedural and historical intel only. No forward-looking convoy dates, routes, loads, or identities. Do not add fields for planned movements.
meta.note_on_dates: date_observed is when the operator experienced/learned the fact; last_verified drives freshness decay (thresholds: amber >30 days, red >90 days).
known_gaps: Name of the correct third Polish crossing was not captured in the interview — claim PL-004 deliberately carries this gap; surfacing it is a feature (the brief shows what needs verifying next).
Exact acronym list for the GB document pack is uncertain in the source ('I honestly don't remember') — GB-002 confidence reflects this.
'WDS' is the operator's rendering of the certificate name; not independently verified against an official form name.

official_rules.claim: Qualifying humanitarian aid goods for Ukraine can leave GB under a simplified process: an oral declaration or declaration by conduct, without a standard customs declaration or EORI, for goods carried in smaller vehicles. Carry a list of the goods.
official_rules.authority: HMRC / GOV.UK — 'Taking humanitarian aid out of Great Britain to support Ukraine'
official_rules.notes: Verify current text the morning of use; guidance framed as an easement and could change.

official_rules.claim: Excluded goods cannot use the simplified process and must be removed or handled separately: controlled goods, medicines not available over the counter without a licence to distribute, dual-use goods, excise goods, military goods, sanctions-related goods.
official_rules.authority: HMRC / GOV.UK — 'Taking humanitarian aid out of Great Britain to support Ukraine'
official_rules.notes: This is the official rule behind the operator's controlled-drugs binning practice (see GB-003).

official_rules.claim: Ukraine operates a State System for Humanitarian Aid with an electronic declaration process intended to accelerate humanitarian clearance; recipient organisations make declarations on the Ukrainian side.
official_rules.authority: Ukrainian government (State System for Humanitarian Aid)
official_rules.notes: Flagged for verification — sourced from secondary research, not read in primary form. Consistent with operator account UA-001.

operator_claims.claim: Since a rule change early in 2026, the UK–France crossing requires a fully itemised list of everything carried plus a T1 transit form, prepared with a paid customs intermediary. The T1 evidences that goods transit the EU without being sold en route.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: They now need a detailed list of everything we send… including what's called a T1 form, which is a transit form… it says what goes into Europe and out the other end, to demonstrate that you haven't sold anything on the way and you don't need to pay tax.

operator_claims.claim: The driver's document pack for leaving GB and transiting Europe includes the T1, a GMR, Channel Tunnel tickets, the vehicle's V5C, and several further reference numbers/acronyms the operator manages via a running email with the customs company (possibly ELO, EMD — uncertain).
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: There's definitely pushing ten three-letter acronyms… there's a GMR, there's an ELO, there's an EMD, I think. I honestly don't remember — I keep them all in a massive email with the customs company.

operator_claims.claim: Practice for donated medicines: check each against the UK controlled list; controlled items are binned, non-controlled items can travel. Items suspected of being dangerous goods (e.g. oxygen concentrators) are declined outright, though without certainty that the classification is correct.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: Someone's asked us to take oxygen concentrators, and I'm pretty sure that's classified as a dangerous item, so I've said no in the past — but if I'm misunderstanding that situation, it would be helpful to know.

operator_claims.claim: The T1 must list every item as a separate line. Filing a bulk total (e.g. 'X kg of humanitarian aid') triggers a requirement for an additional security certificate (rendered by the operator as 'WDS'); without it, vehicles are stopped at the Polish border.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: The T1 form has to have every item listed, not just a bulk amount… if you don't have all the items individually listed, you have to get an additional certificate, which is called a WDS form. We did the itemised list this time and went through the right border and it all worked.
operator_claims.notes: Confirmed empirically by the successful July crossing after switching to itemised listing. The Polish embassy did not recognise the WDS form (see FR-003).

operator_claims.claim: Customs intermediaries default to bulk filing because they charge per line item and bulk is cheaper — and they will ask the charity what it wants filed rather than advising. Instruct them explicitly to itemise every line.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: They were like, 'what would you like us to do?' And you're like — I don't know, you're the expert here… so you end up saying, well, this is what ChatGPT tells me is my preference, and then you're not sure if it's right or not.

operator_claims.claim: The Polish embassy, when consulted, did not recognise the 'WDS' certificate and advised that a fully itemised list was probably sufficient — which subsequently proved correct.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: The Polish embassy didn't know what it was. They were like, 'I don't think you need it… I think if you're fully item-listed, that's fine.'

operator_claims.claim: The pedestrian crossing at Medyka, previously used by the convoy, began turning humanitarian vehicles away ('you're at the wrong border') without explaining which crossing was correct.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: They kept saying you're at the wrong border. They never really explained which border we were meant to be at.

operator_claims.claim: Each Polish crossing applies different regulations for humanitarian vehicles, and these change over time; much of the operative knowledge circulates by word of mouth and is not reliably published anywhere online — general-purpose AI tools fail on these questions for that reason.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: Each border has different regulations and they keep changing, and there's a lot of word-of-mouth stuff going on, so it's not on the internet. When you use ChatGPT to try and determine which one it is, it doesn't do a very good job — there's basically no recorded reliable internet information on it.

operator_claims.claim: A third crossing (NAME NOT CAPTURED — needs follow-up) is currently the correct one for humanitarian aid vehicles. It previously carried a 3.5-tonne vehicle limit, since raised to 7 tonnes. Confirmed by a successful crossing in July 2026.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: We now know that there's a third border which is the right one for humanitarian aid… that border technically had a restriction of 3.5 tonnes going through it, but they've now changed it and upgraded it to 7. I don't know if that's recorded anywhere.
operator_claims.notes: Deliberate gap: crossing name unknown. In the UI this renders as 'needs verification — ask the next operator who crosses'. The threshold-change portion is at the boundary of first-hand and unrecorded official change; kept medium.

operator_claims.claim: An agency located at the Polish border can complete missing customs paperwork for a fee, but is not reliable (computer system down on one occasion). Escalation path that worked: the duty manager telephoned the border guard, who allowed the convoy through.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: There's an agency very conveniently located right at the Polish border and you can give them a stack of money… apart from the fact that on this occasion their computer system had shut down. So we spoke to the duty manager, and he rings up the border guard and says, it's okay, just let them through.
operator_claims.notes: Anecdote of a one-off workaround — present as 'reported escalation path', never as a recommended procedure.

operator_claims.claim: Smaller humanitarian vehicles use a separate queue from lorries at the Polish border. Typical crossing time with correct paperwork is around half a day; the missing-certificate incident cost the best part of a full day. Lorry queues reportedly run to days (second-hand).
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: You're in a humanitarian aid queue, not a lorry queue… it's relatively quick, some sort of hours, sort of a half day at the border. Lorries can be there for days from what I hear — I've never done it, it's just hearsay.
operator_claims.notes: hearsay=true applies to the lorry-queue portion only; the half-day figure is first-hand.

operator_claims.claim: Ukraine-side declarations are made by trusted recipient organisations, not the UK sender. Recipients need from the sender: what is being delivered, item details, and vehicle information. The process involves a request-letter registration and an acceptance letter at the end, both of which need chasing.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: Declarations are done by them… more they need information from us: what we're delivering, information about the vehicle — it's what allows them to do their declaration. There's a lot of communication, walking them through doing the declarations and checking — have you done the declaration?

operator_claims.claim: The Ukraine border document pack (declaration, vehicle V5C, lead driver's passport, and others) is printed in the UK and physically handed to drivers at the Polish border by the organiser, who flies out to meet the convoy. It is also considered advisable to email documentation to the Polish border in advance.
operator_claims.verbatim_quote: I meet them at the Polish border — I typically fly to Poland on a cheap flight — and then there's another stack of documents for the Ukraine border… there's also an email that it's advisable to send to the Polish border.

demo_debrief_2.purpose: Second debrief for the live merge demo. Written to produce one CORROBORATION (FR-001), one SUPERSESSION-candidate/CONFLICT (PL-004 threshold), and one NEW single-report claim. Label clearly as synthetic in any slide notes; never present as real evidence.
demo_debrief_2.raw_text: Just back from our August run, two vans via the tunnel. The customs company tried to talk us into a bulk declaration again to save money — we insisted on line-by-line on the T1 after hearing what happened to another group, and we cleared the Polish side in about five hours, no issues. One thing though: the crossing we used told us the vehicle limit is 5 tonnes now, not 7 — the guard said it changed at the start of August. Also worth knowing: they've started asking for the recipient organisation's registration number at the Polish side, not just the Ukrainian side — we had it in the email thread luckily, but it wasn't on any checklist we'd seen.

expected_merge_outcomes.effect: 7t (verified Jul, first-hand) vs 5t (Aug, first-hand report of a guard's statement). Similar recency, contradictory → status → conflicting; UI surfaces both with dates and lets the operator decide / flags for verification. This is the money shot of the merge demo.
New claim: Polish side now requesting recipient organisation's registration number. status → single_report, confidence medium.
